docs.title: The Sum Function in C++
docs.text:
Author(s):

(RGB) Raghav B. Venkataramaiyer <bv.raghav -at- thapar -dot- edu>

This project creates a sum function in c++ as a sample to illustrate how to compile a shared library and distribute it for use along with the binary.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
make -C code

This will create create a folder dist in code folder, with following contents

dist
 +-lib
 |  \-libbvr_math.so
 +-bin
    \-run

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
cd code
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=dist/lib
./dist/bin/run

docs.title: Phase-one data-source register
docs.text:
Checked on 9 September 2026. The application stores small, manually curated snapshots; it does not copy entire datasets or call these services live.

Prototype records Publisher/source URL Use in Phase 1 PM-KISAN, AB PM-JAY, PMAY-U, PMUY, PM SVANidhi, DHTESS, JSY myScheme, Digital India Corporation https://www.myscheme.gov.in/ Names, responsible organisation, broad purpose and source links. Atal Pension Yojana Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority https://pfrda.org.in/web/pfrda/schemes/atal-pension-yojana-apy Broad purpose, target audience and source link. PIN-code examples OGD Platform India, Department of Posts https://www.data.gov.in/resource/all-india-pincode-directory-till-last-month Three demonstration location records.

docs.title: Data-use rules
docs.text:
• Only stable summary fields are shown; detailed eligibility and benefit amounts are deliberately omitted.
  • Each record carries a source URL and last_verified date.
  • The portal says “potentially relevant,” not “eligible.”
  • Users are directed to the official source before applying or acting.
  • No citizen answers, identity numbers or personal profiles are stored.
  • Restricted sources and identity-verification services are outside project scope.

docs.title: Department of Posts PIN directory import
docs.text:
The OGD catalogue identifies the PIN directory as open access and describes office, PIN, district and state fields. The resource page identifies the Department of Posts as the publisher. The platform identifies its published data as subject to the Government Open Data License - India, which requires attribution and contains further conditions. Review the dataset's current terms before reuse.

The optional CSV adapter imports a file obtained separately from that official resource page; it does not download the data itself or authenticate to the API. The operator must verify the file, its provenance and date. The adapter retains the provider, resource URL and licence on each record, groups all offices under each PIN and rejects the entire batch if a required row is malformed. office_name, district and state represent the first sorted office for compatibility; the offices array contains all offices in the imported file for that PIN. Imports upsert PINs. Prior records owned by this adapter but absent from a later file are retained and marked for review, not deleted; a partial file can cause omitted records to be marked for review. No official CSV has been bundled.

On 5 November 2026, the resource page published the expected headers officename, pincode, district and statename, but its linked CSV returned HTTP 403 when requested. No downloaded snapshot was verified or imported during this check; the adapter tests use synthetic fixtures. An optional scripts.fetch_ogd_pincode downloader accepts an operator-supplied resource UUID and API key for the official API host and writes a new CSV for review. It has only been tested with simulated responses, not the live PIN API. Stable reported totals do not prove that offset pages formed a consistent snapshot, nor that the supplied UUID is the PIN resource. The operator must independently verify resource identity, completeness, date and terms before import. The OGD platform's help page describes API-key generation for registered users. No user API key has been requested or stored by this project. A locally downloaded, independently verified CSV remains an alternative for the existing adapter.

On 23 November 2026, the OGD resource listing identified the resource UUID as 5c2f62fe-5afa-4119-a499-fec9d604d5bd. The listed public CSV link returned HTTP 403 again. The IndiaAI AIKosh listing points to that same OGD resource. A full current monthly file remains unavailable in this environment. The PIN adapters now store the SHA-256 of each newly imported file with the record provenance. The manual official importer can match it against an operator-reviewed digest. When trimming changes a PIN, office, district or state value, the office keeps the original text under original_values. Equivalent office entries still share one normalized office record.

docs.title: Department of Posts May 2019 archive
docs.text:
On 25 November 2026, the official archive URL served a CSV with 155,599 rows and 19,252 distinct six-digit PINs. The India Data Platform catalogue record identifies the Department of Posts as the publisher, cites this official file, and lists the same 16,431,380-byte size. The archive contains legacy geographic names. The importer uses the archive date for provenance and leaves the current verification date empty. Both the public page and the API indicate that the record requires review. The raw CSV remains in the ignored data/raw/ folder.

Department of Posts, 2019, All India Pincode Directory, Open Government Data Platform India, 30/05. Published under the Government Open Data License - India. Official CSV · Licence

The archive adapter checks SHA-256 e2fc773ebc697bb5aa96b76b6a38a2289d450e896769550259df89a2afe54c90 and decodes the pinned bytes with Windows-1252 for six nonbreaking-space characters. It groups offices by PIN, collapses repeated office tuples, and retains original values changed by trimming.

docs.title: Historical third-party mirror
docs.text: On 14 November 2026 a 2024 GitHub mirror was downloaded because the official download was unavailable. The repository claims the data originated from the OGD directory, but the bytes have not been independently compared with the government file. The dedicated mirror adapter pins the file checksum and keeps the mirror URL, claimed original URL and repository licence in every record. The mirror commit date is stored as snapshot_date, not as an official verification date; last_verified is null. All imported records remain review_due with reason unverified_mirror. Do not use this snapshot to claim current postal availability. The raw CSV and its local provenance note are excluded from Git by the data/raw/ ignore rule. For matching PINs, the mirror adapter preserves records owned by other adapters or with unknown ownership. It updates only its own prior records and reports the count actually applied.

docs.title: PIB JanSamarth scheme snapshot
docs.text:
The Ministry of Finance release published by PIB on 30 March 2026 lists 15 credit-linked schemes. The adapter imports 14 names and ministries from that table, omitting PM SVANidhi because it is already in the default catalogue. PIB's copyright policy permits reproduction subject to accurate, non-misleading use and attribution, with third-party material excluded. The snapshot includes the publisher, release and policy URLs.

The release is historical, not a live dataset. Records use the release date as a conservative verification date and are explicitly marked review_due; current availability, geographic scope, eligibility and benefits must be checked independently. Categories and tags are local discovery labels, while states and audiences are left empty when the table does not establish them. The adapter performs no live scraping and does not claim complete coverage of the 15 schemes.

docs.title: PIB transport snapshot
docs.text: The 28 July 2026 Ministry of Heavy Industries release describes PM E-DRIVE's electric mobility and charging objectives and records different dates for individual vehicle segments. BharatOS transcribes one broad description, labels it review_due, and leaves state and audience fields unspecified. The publication date is used as a conservative verification date; the record does not establish present availability or eligibility. The same PIB copyright policy linked above applies. This is a manually curated historical snapshot, not a live feed or a complete transport dataset.

docs.title: PIB environment snapshot
docs.text: The 30 July 2026 Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change release describes National Clean Air Programme action plans in 130 cities. The record is a dated, manually curated programme summary, marked review_due and not a live coverage list. The source does not describe an individual payment or application process. States and audiences are left unspecified rather than implying that every location is covered. PIB's policy above applies.

docs.title: PIB health, education, employment and agriculture snapshots
docs.text:
The linked releases were checked on 23 November 2026. These summaries retain the publication date separately from the date the link and its contents were checked. Records remain review_due because the releases describe past programme information. Audience tags support discovery. Current eligibility, geographic availability and enrolment require confirmation from the responsible authority.

Records Publisher and release Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 11 August 2026 Samagra Shiksha and NIPUN Bharat Mission Ministry of Education, 10 August 2026 Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana Ministry of Labour and Employment, 19 June 2026 National Mission on Natural Farming Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, 24 March 2026

The project stores brief paraphrases with attribution and a link to the PIB copyright policy. The importer runs entirely from the curated local snapshots.

The public scheme filter also lists the states and union territories from the Integrated Government Online Directory. The presence of a region in the selector does not establish programme coverage there. Matches still use the scope recorded in each scheme snapshot.

docs.title: 60-second project explanation
docs.text: BharatOS is a student-built portal and API for Indian public schemes and civic data. Government information is spread across portals with different formats and access methods. Citizens can search source-linked scheme snapshots without creating a profile. Developers can use versioned endpoints; in database mode they can register, create and revoke keys, and view usage. The project now also includes database-backed imports, optional Redis caching and limits, and administrator monitoring. When available, detail pages show the last administrator-run check of the exact source page, including its time; that check does not prove the data is current. The available records are still limited snapshots, not a complete live government feed. The diagrams describe the intended full system, while the table below distinguishes implemented and planned features.

docs.title: Problem, solution and value
docs.text:
• Problem: useful government data exists, but it is fragmented across departments, formats, naming conventions and access mechanisms.
  • Solution: a thin normalization and developer-experience layer that keeps the official source visible.
  • Citizen value: faster discovery of potentially relevant schemes without creating a profile.
  • Developer value: one versioned response structure rather than a new integration for every source.
  • Administrative value: one place to monitor source availability, ingestion runs, freshness and API health.
  • Important boundary: BharatOS is not an official service and never makes a final eligibility decision.

docs.title: What each interface does
docs.text:
1. Explore schemes: searches and filters the currently loaded source-linked records by text, category, state and audience. When selected state or audience filters hide records with unspecified relevant metadata, the page reports how many may need separate review; a checkbox can include and label them. Missing metadata is not an eligibility decision. The default in-memory catalogue has eight records; database imports may add others.
  2. Scheme details: explains the broad purpose, possible relevance, responsible ministry, source and verification date.
  3. Developer console: uses a fixed demo key in in-memory mode. In database mode, developers register, sign in, create, rotate and revoke personal keys, view usage and call the API playground.
  4. API documentation: /docs explains the contract; /reference and /openapi.json provide the generated API reference and schema.
  5. Admin view: with a configured administrator token and database, displays recorded runs, quality indicators, usage totals, optional cache metrics and explicitly requested source-page checks. These checks do not prove dataset availability or current eligibility.
  6. PIN lookup: allows anonymous searches over loaded location records, displays all offices in a record and highlights third-party or stale provenance. PINs may still appear in the browser URL/history; server access logs redact the query.

docs.title: Identified actors
docs.text: Actor Why the actor is outside the system Main interactions Public User Uses public features without needing an account. Search/filter schemes, view details, check potential fit and look up PIN codes. Registered Developer Is a specialized user who also has developer credentials. Sign in, manage API keys, read docs, test/call APIs and view usage. Administrator Operates the platform. Manage sources, trigger ingestion, monitor freshness and review abuse. Government Data Source An external system supplying permitted records. Provides datasets or API responses to ingestion. Scheduler An external time-based trigger. Starts scheduled ingestion runs.

docs.title: Use Case Diagram
docs.text:
The diagram answers “who can ask BharatOS to do what?” The large rectangle is the system boundary. Actors remain outside it. The internal use cases are grouped into citizen discovery, developer platform and data operations.

Relationship justification:

  • Registered Developer --|> Public User is actor generalization: a registered developer may also use public discovery features, whether or not signed in.
  • “View scheme details” includes “Review source and freshness” because every detail response must show provenance.
  • “Manage API keys” includes session authentication because each key operation checks the developer's session. Registering or signing in is a separate use case; a valid existing session avoids signing in again.
  • In the target design, “Call versioned API” includes key validation, rate-limit enforcement and provenance. The current implementation enforces rate limits only when Redis is configured; the in-memory demonstration mode does not provide rate limiting.
  • “Test an endpoint” includes “Call versioned API” because the playground uses the same public contract.
  • Ingestion includes normalization and deduplication as distinct mandatory steps in the target pipeline.
  • No extend relationship is used merely to decorate the diagram. Optional exceptional paths are clearer in the activity and sequence diagrams.

docs.title: Major use cases to explain verbally
docs.text:
• Search and filter schemes: anonymous query over canonical metadata.
  • View provenance: source name, URL, last verification and freshness state are part of the result.
  • Call versioned API: a developer supplies a key and receives a standard envelope.
  • Manage API keys: create, rotate and revoke credentials in database mode.
  • Ingest source data: collect only from permitted APIs/files and record the source version.
  • Monitor freshness: detect failed runs or stale records rather than silently presenting them as current.

docs.title: Class Diagram
docs.text:
This is the static/domain view. NormalizedRecord captures fields shared by data exposed through the platform. Scheme and Location inherit from it. SourceMetadata is composed into each normalized record because provenance must travel with the record. A scheme owns one or more EligibilityRule objects. A DeveloperAccount owns zero or more ApiKey objects, and keys authorize request logs. DataSourceAdapter is an interface implemented by API/file adapters.

Key multiplicities:

  • One developer account owns 0..* keys; a new account may have none, while active developers may rotate several.
  • One key can authorize 0..* requests; each logged protected request refers to one key.
  • One dataset contains 0..* normalized records; an empty new dataset is valid before its first successful run.
  • One data source publishes 1..* datasets and produces 0..* ingestion runs.
  • One scheme composes 1..* eligibility rules; deleting the scheme removes those scheme-specific rules.

docs.title: Sequence Diagram
docs.text: This is the target runtime/time-ordered view for a protected API request. The gateway validates the key and checks quota before using a cache or the data service. The alt fragments show invalid-key, rate-limit, cache-hit and cache-miss paths. In the current database mode, key validation and the cache revision check still query the database on a cache hit; the cache avoids loading the full scheme catalogue, not every database access. PIN lookups use the database directly. Redis and limits are optional in local development.

docs.title: Activity Diagram
docs.text: This is the target control-flow view of ingestion. It has paths for collection, validation, quarantine, deduplication and publication. Today a failed batch publishes zero records. The last good data remains available with review_due status. Each failed run records a diagnostic code and the first offending record or CSV line when known. Keep the original snapshot for investigation. After correcting the adapter or obtaining a corrected snapshot, repeat the import. Configurable thresholds and selective release of quarantined records remain planned.

docs.title: Component Diagram
docs.text: This is the high-level architecture view. Browser experiences depend on the API gateway. The gateway delegates identity, canonical data access, cache/rate limits and logging. Ingestion is separate from live request serving, so a failed source refresh does not directly break the API. PostgreSQL owns durable normalized data, while Redis owns disposable cache and rate-limit state.

docs.title: Why multiple diagrams are necessary
docs.text:
• Use case: requirements and actor responsibilities.
  • Class: domain structure and data relationships.
  • Sequence: order of interactions for one request.
  • Activity: branching process logic for ingestion.
  • Component: system modules and technical dependencies.

No single diagram can accurately represent all five concerns without becoming unreadable.

docs.title: Original Phase 1 architecture
docs.text:
• FastAPI receives page and API requests.
  • Jinja renders accessible server-side pages.
  • Pydantic validates scheme, location, source and response-envelope data.
  • Python lists provide eight scheme snapshots and three PIN-code records.
  • A FastAPI dependency checks the fixed prototype X-API-Key.
  • Search filters run in memory and do not save request profiles.
  • Minimal browser JavaScript controls navigation, key copying and the API playground.
  • Pytest/TestClient verify page routes and API behaviour.

docs.title: Current implementation beyond Phase 1
docs.text:
• Setting DATABASE_URL switches scheme and PIN reads to SQLite or PostgreSQL; Alembic manages the schema.
  • The ingestion pipeline stores source attribution, tracks runs, rejects invalid batches and advances a cache revision. A dated PIB scheme subset is available; a PIN CSV adapter and optional scheduler require an independently verified local file.
  • Database-backed filters use stored scheme metadata indexes for category, state and audience. Free-text substring search currently uses SQL LIKE; it is not yet a full-text search engine and individual searches are not saved by the index.
  • Database mode provides developer accounts, hashed keys, rotation/revocation, expiring sessions and request logs. The fixed demo key works only without a configured database.
  • Configured Redis provides scheme-catalogue caching and fixed-window request limits. PIN lookups query the database directly. Without Redis, these features are disabled.
  • The protected administrator view shows recorded runs, freshness and quality indicators, cache counters, alerts and manually triggered HEAD checks of fixed official pages.
  • A local Compose stack, optional localhost HTTPS, backup/restore tooling and measured prototype/service benchmarks are available. Public deployment and a developer pilot have not been completed.

docs.title: Target architecture
docs.text:
1. Ingestion: a source-specific adapter reads a permitted public API or file.
  2. Validation: required fields, types and source constraints are checked.
  3. Normalization: source-specific names become canonical fields while originals remain traceable.
  4. Deduplication: deterministic keys prevent the same civic entity being served twice.
  5. Provenance enrichment: source, retrieval time, update time and freshness status are attached.
  6. Storage: a successful batch is committed atomically to PostgreSQL.
  7. Serving: the gateway validates the key and rate limit, checks Redis and queries the service on a miss.
  8. Feedback: request and ingestion metrics feed developer/admin dashboards.

docs.title: Standard API contract
docs.text:
Successful responses use:

{
  "data": {},
  "meta": {
    "api_version": "v1",
    "environment": "prototype",
    "source": "Publisher or source set",
    "last_verified": "2026-09-09",
    "generated_at": "ISO-8601 timestamp",
    "result_count": 1
  }
}

Errors use:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "INVALID_API_KEY",
    "message": "Human-readable explanation",
    "request_id": "Traceable identifier"
  }
}

The envelope lets clients handle success, metadata and errors consistently across datasets. /v1 protects existing clients when a future incompatible schema requires /v2.

docs.title: Why Python-first
docs.text: The proposal initially suggested a Next.js/Node.js implementation. Phase 1 uses FastAPI, Jinja and Pydantic instead because the same language can serve the portal, API, validation, ingestion adapters, tests and future data processing. Server-rendered templates reduce frontend build complexity, while small JavaScript modules preserve interactive quality. The architectural boundaries and REST contract remain independent of the implementation language.

docs.title: Why PostgreSQL and Redis are useful
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL provides transactions, constraints, indexing, relational modelling and JSON fields for heterogeneous source metadata.
  • Redis is appropriate for temporary cached responses and atomic rate-limit counters.
  • Keeping Redis disposable prevents cache state from becoming the source of truth.
  • Both are now supported in the local Compose stack. The original in-memory mode remains available for a quick demonstration.

docs.title: Security, privacy and legal boundaries
docs.text:
• Production API keys must be random, shown once and stored only as secure hashes.
  • HTTPS is required outside localhost.
  • Rate limits protect availability but do not replace authentication or authorization.
  • Citizen search remains anonymous; BharatOS does not need identity numbers to suggest broad scheme categories.
  • Uvicorn access logs redact client addresses, query strings and dynamic paths. Browser history and external proxy logs are separate and need their own privacy controls.
  • Aadhaar, PAN, driving-licence verification and restricted databases are explicitly outside scope.
  • Only permitted public/open sources may be ingested.
  • Source ownership and licence must be recorded per dataset.
  • Cached stale records must be labelled stale; the system must never silently claim that old data is current.

docs.title: Part 5: Current versus planned functionality
docs.text: Capability Current status Remaining work Scheme discovery and details Eight in-memory snapshots and 29 schemes in a freshly seeded local database, including records from six sectors covered by the dated PIB imports Broader, permitted official datasets and improved discovery Versioned API and standard envelope In-memory or database-backed local endpoints Expand dataset coverage and production hardening Developer access Database mode supports accounts, expiring sessions and hashed, rotatable/revocable keys Account recovery, security review and production controls PIN-code lookup Three demonstration records; CSV adapter, checked local-file scheduler and an optional historical mirror tested with 19,300 PINs A verified official full dataset import Developer analytics Persisted authenticated-request totals in database mode Further analysis and operational evaluation Admin monitoring Token-protected recorded runs, freshness, quality, cache metrics, dashboard alerts and on-demand HEAD checks Notification delivery, history and richer operations PostgreSQL and Redis Supported and tested with local Compose services Ongoing security and operational review Scheduled ingestion Optional scheduler checks one operator-approved local PIN snapshot Wider source scheduling and independently verified inputs Performance results Local in-memory and PostgreSQL/Redis concurrency runs recorded Repeated tests with larger datasets and a real developer pilot Deployment Local Compose, optional localhost HTTPS and backup/restore drill Public deployment, public certificates, security and operational ownership

docs.title: Part 6: Five-minute lab demonstration
docs.text:
1. 0:00–0:40 — Problem and boundary: state the fragmentation problem, hybrid citizen/developer goal and student-project disclaimer.
  2. 0:40–1:30 — Citizen flow: search “health,” apply an audience filter, open a result and point out source/freshness and the non-eligibility warning.
  3. 1:30–2:30 — Developer flow: in default mode use the demo key; in database mode sign in and create a personal key. Run the scheme list and, if the demonstration records were seeded, PIN 147004; show the envelope.
  4. 2:30–3:05 — Error behaviour: explain or demonstrate that a missing key returns a standard 401 error.
  5. 3:05–3:40 — Admin boundary: if configured, load the dashboard with the administrator token; distinguish recorded import results and optional HEAD checks from a live guarantee of dataset availability.
  6. 3:40–4:45 — UML: use the use case diagram for requirements, sequence for live requests and activity for ingestion; mention what class/component diagrams add.
  7. 4:45–5:00 — Roadmap: identify the verified official PIN import, wider source coverage, production security and developer pilot as remaining work.

docs.title: Part 7: Likely viva questions and answers
1. What is the primary goal of BharatOS?
docs.text:
Short: To reduce the effort required to discover and integrate permitted Indian public schemes and civic data.

Technical: It creates a canonical domain model and versioned REST contract above source-specific adapters while preserving provenance and freshness.

docs.title: 2. Is BharatOS replacing government portals?
docs.text: No. Official publishers remain the authority and application destination. BharatOS is a discovery and normalization layer that links back to them.

docs.title: 3. Why are citizens anonymous?
docs.text: Broad discovery needs category, state and audience filters, not a stored identity profile. This minimizes personal-data risk and keeps Phase 1 within course scope.

docs.title: 4. Why is “potential fit” different from eligibility?
docs.text: Eligibility may depend on detailed rules, documents, official databases and changing policy. The system can narrow discovery but should not claim an authoritative decision.

docs.title: 5. Why use a Use Case Diagram?
docs.text: It establishes the system boundary, identifies external actors and connects each actor to functional requirements without describing implementation details.

docs.title: 6. What is the difference between include and extend?
docs.text: include means the included behaviour is a required reusable part of the base use case. extend means optional or conditional behaviour adds to a complete base use case. This diagram uses include only where the child behaviour always occurs.

docs.title: 7. Why is Registered Developer a specialization of Public User?
docs.text: A developer can perform all anonymous discovery actions and has additional authenticated developer capabilities. The hollow-triangle generalization points to the more general actor.

docs.title: 8. Why use composition for source metadata?
docs.text: Provenance is inseparable from the normalized record exposed by BharatOS. A record without source/freshness metadata violates the API contract.

docs.title: 9. Why use an adapter interface?
docs.text: Every source has different formats and access mechanisms. Adapters isolate those differences behind collect, parse, validate and normalize, so adding a source does not rewrite the API layer.

docs.title: 10. Why separate ingestion from request serving?
docs.text: Ingestion is scheduled and failure-prone; serving is latency-sensitive. Decoupling allows the API to continue with explicitly stale last-known data when a source is temporarily unavailable.

docs.title: 11. Why are API endpoints versioned?
docs.text: Versioning prevents an incompatible schema change from silently breaking existing developer applications. Additive compatible changes can remain in v1; breaking changes require v2.

docs.title: 12. Why have a standard response envelope?
docs.text: Clients always know where to find data, provenance, version, timestamps and machine-readable errors, regardless of the dataset.

docs.title: 13. Why hash API keys?
docs.text: Like passwords, raw keys should not be recoverable from the database. The server hashes the presented key and compares it with the stored hash. Phase 1's visible fixed key is only a demonstration.

docs.title: 14. What is the role of Redis?
docs.text: Redis holds short-lived response cache entries and atomic rate-limit counters. PostgreSQL remains the durable source of truth.

docs.title: 15. How is stale data handled?
docs.text: The ingestion run records source and retrieval timestamps. If refresh fails, last-known data may remain available only with an explicit stale status; it must not be presented as current.

docs.title: 16. How do you avoid duplicate records?
docs.text: Use deterministic matching keys and source-specific reconciliation rules, retain original identifiers and record merge decisions. Ambiguous records should be quarantined instead of guessed.

docs.title: 17. What testing is present now?
docs.text: Unit and integration tests cover validation, filtering, page and API routes, key lifecycle, ingestion, migrations, monitoring and caching. PostgreSQL and Redis service tests are also available; see the evaluation notes for actual runs.

docs.title: 18. How has performance been evaluated?
docs.text: Local tests at 10, 50, 100 and 500 concurrent requests recorded p95 latency, error rate and provenance coverage for both prototype and PostgreSQL/Redis configurations. These were short local runs, not production capacity claims. See docs/evaluation/README.md; the developer pilot remains outstanding.

docs.title: 19. Why FastAPI and Jinja?
docs.text: FastAPI provides typed request handling and OpenAPI-compatible models; Pydantic validates contracts; Jinja provides a lightweight, accessible server-rendered interface. Most of the stack remains Python without sacrificing a polished browser experience.

docs.title: 20. What is the most important project risk?
docs.text: Trust. Incorrect, stale or unauthorized data could harm users. The design therefore treats permissions, validation, provenance, freshness and honest failure states as core requirements rather than optional metadata.

docs.title: Final points to remember in the lab
docs.text:
• Say prototype snapshot, not live government integration.
  • Say potentially relevant, not eligible.
  • Point to the source and verification date on the interface.
  • Explain that the UML models the complete target system and the phase table identifies current implementation.
  • Distinguish the implemented local PostgreSQL/Redis and monitoring features from production-ready deployment, and cite only measured evaluation results.

docs.title: Status as of 25 November 2026
docs.text:
This roadmap describes the full target, not a claim that every item is complete. Phase 1 is implemented. Database models, migrations, curated snapshot imports, optional PostgreSQL/Redis, developer access, local monitoring, one checked-file scheduler, local HTTPS and backup tooling have been added in later phases. Structured database search indexes are in place; free-text substring search still uses SQL LIKE. The official May 2019 PIN archive is available for historical use. The current monthly PIN dataset and a live PIB feed remain unavailable. Wider source coverage, an external developer pilot, production security review and deployment remain incomplete. Local test and measurement evidence is in evaluation.

Compose can use a restricted PostgreSQL web login. Schema migrations, ingestion and database backups still run under their existing operator connections.

The current local stack was evaluated with 24 scheme records, 19,300 PIN records and both forms of the scheme-list API. The evaluation includes measured latency, errors, dated provenance coverage and the developer key flow.

A separate July 2026 PIB transport snapshot adds one review-due PM E-DRIVE record; it does not constitute complete transport coverage or establish current benefit availability. An additional dated PIB environment snapshot describes the National Clean Air Programme as city-level action; it does not imply an individual benefit or complete environment coverage. Four further PIB releases add five health, education, employment and agriculture records through the existing scheme schema and ingestion pipeline. The source register lists the publications and dates. These additions expand sector coverage with dated snapshots. The packaged PostgreSQL importer was run twice and retained five records across the four sources. The full PostgreSQL and Redis test run passed 149 tests with the expanded seed.

A third-party 2024 PIN-directory mirror was tested with 19,300 PINs in isolated databases. Its origin and current accuracy have not been independently verified against the monthly official file. Use the source register for the separately verified official historical download and its date.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Interactive prototype and software design
docs.text:
Purpose: make the system understandable, demonstrable and testable before infrastructure work begins.

Delivered in this repository:

  • FastAPI/Jinja multi-page portal.
  • Anonymous scheme discovery and details.
  • Developer console with a working API playground.
  • Read-only administrator preview.
  • Three normalized prototype endpoints.
  • Pydantic contracts and standardized errors.
  • Use case, class, sequence, activity and component diagrams.
  • Automated tests and Software Engineering Lab guide.

Exit criterion: a reviewer can start the project locally, complete the demonstration flow and explain how phase-one code maps to the target architecture.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Data and normalization foundation
docs.text:
• Introduce PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy and Alembic migrations.
  • Implement repository and service boundaries around canonical records.
  • Define and implement the DataSourceAdapter contract.
  • Track each imported dataset's record kind and snapshot policy in a canonical registry.
  • Ingest one permitted official scheme dataset and one location/PIN-code dataset.
  • Validate, normalize, deduplicate and attach source/freshness metadata.
  • Replace static API data with database-backed queries.

Exit criterion: a reproducible ingestion run produces validated records that the versioned API serves end to end.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Developer access and API gateway
docs.text:
• Add developer registration, login and secure sessions.
  • Generate, hash, rotate and revoke API keys.
  • Add Redis-backed response caching and per-key rate limiting.
  • Persist request logs and expose real usage metrics.
  • Generate an OpenAPI reference from the implemented contract.

Exit criterion: a new developer can register, create a key, call the API, see usage and prove that an invalid or revoked key is rejected.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Dataset expansion and discovery quality
docs.text:
• Add adapters for health, education, employment, agriculture, transport and environment data.
  • Add scheduled ingestion, source-specific validation and search indexing.
  • Introduce dataset quality scoring for freshness, completeness and consistency.
  • Expand anonymous potential-fit filters without saving citizen profiles.
  • Surface source outages and stale records clearly.

Exit criterion: multiple source adapters publish through the same canonical contract without changing consumer integrations.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Operations, testing and evaluation
docs.text:
• Connect the administrator dashboard to real ingestion, freshness and source-health data.
  • Add monitoring, alerts, cache metrics and error analysis.
  • Complete unit, integration, security and performance suites.
  • Measure concurrency at 10, 50, 100 and 500 requests.
  • Conduct and document a developer time-to-first-call pilot.

Exit criterion: the functional suite passes and p95 latency, error rate, provenance coverage and pilot results are recorded from repeatable runs.

docs.title: Phase 6 — Deployment and optional extensions
docs.text:
• Add Docker Compose, CI checks, environment-based secrets and deployment documentation.
  • Configure TLS, backups, recovery and operational ownership.
  • Review data permissions and licences before publication.
  • Consider a Python SDK, GraphQL, multilingual metadata and geospatial queries only after the REST core meets its evaluation targets.

Exit criterion: the system can be deployed reproducibly and operated without hiding failures, stale data or source limitations.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
The application workflow installs headless Chromium and runs the browser and PostgreSQL/Redis tests alongside the default suite. It also runs tests/test_compose_deployment.py::test_compose_https_with_restricted_database_role against the localhost HTTPS profile. That test recovers a PostgreSQL backup, confirms keys and logs through the restored application, and verifies that a subsequent backup includes post-recovery writes. tests/test_database_backup.py covers failed dumps, destination races and restore preflight. To enable the browser tests locally:

uv sync --frozen
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m playwright install --only-shell chromium
$env:RUN_BROWSER_TESTS = "1"
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests/test_browser_workflows.py -q

The automated PIN CSV tests use fixtures, and the PostgreSQL API test uses a seeded canonical PIN. The source register records the separate official archive verification. The current monthly directory import and volunteer evaluation remain open.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: BharatOS UML diagrams
docs.text:
This folder contains the editable PlantUML source and the verified SVG/PNG renders for the complete planned BharatOS system.

Diagram Why it is included Use case Defines the system boundary, external actors and services available to each actor. Class Defines the main domain entities, multiplicities, compositions, inheritance and adapter interface. Sequence Explains the ordered runtime interactions for a protected API request. Activity Explains control flow, decisions and failure paths in data ingestion. Component Separates deployable responsibilities and shows dependencies on storage and official sources.

Regenerate all assets from the project root:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\render_diagrams.py

The renderer fails when the PlantUML server returns a syntax-error SVG, a dimensionless SVG or an invalid PNG. The final assets should also be visually reviewed before submission.

docs.title: 25 November official archive import
docs.text: Two consecutive imports of the May 2019 Department of Posts archive into an isolated PostgreSQL 17 database each accepted 19,252 PINs. The database retained 19,252 distinct location records after both runs. An authenticated request for 515631 returned 15 offices, the official download URL, the file checksum, the archive date and review_due status. The response's last_verified remained empty because current details were unverified. The SQLite localhost launcher also imported all 19,252 PINs in a separate database.

docs.title: 23 November Compose evaluation
docs.text:
The 23 November 2026 run used a Windows client and one Docker-hosted Uvicorn worker built from 986aa17, with PostgreSQL 17 and Redis 7. The isolated database contained 24 schemes from the curated and PIB adapters and 19,300 PINs, including the historical third-party mirror. The benchmark exercised the scheme list. A separate authenticated PIN lookup returned 15 offices for 515631 with mirror provenance and a null verification date.

Concurrency p95, full list p95, 12-record page 10 48.97 ms 44.40 ms 50 302.26 ms 450.37 ms 100 1,325.76 ms 1,296.56 ms 500 2,328.55 ms 2,044.31 ms

All 500 requests at every level succeeded in each run. Every successful response contained a nonempty result set and dated source metadata in the envelope and each returned record. This metric measures the presence of provenance fields. Some sources are historical and still require review. The paged API reads through the database, while the full-list API uses the Redis catalogue cache. The runs were sequential, once per endpoint, and used different response sizes and access paths. The local test suite was running during the start of the full-list run. At 500 concurrent requests, both runs exceeded two seconds at p95. These results describe one local configuration, and the PIN endpoint has no concurrency results from this run.

An automated HTTP check registered a test account, signed in, created a key and made calls to the list and PIN endpoints. Usage reported all 4,005 authenticated requests, including warm-ups and smoke calls. The admin endpoint reported the expected record counts and 2,001 cache hits, one miss and zero cache errors. The revoked key received HTTP 401. The separate developer pilot still requires observations from volunteers.

The complete test suite passed all 149 tests in a Linux container against the seeded PostgreSQL and Redis services, including the populated PostgreSQL migration and Redis cache checks. The test stack and its disposable volume were removed after verification.

Raw data is available for the full list and 12-record page. To repeat, start an isolated Compose project, apply migrations and import the curated, JanSamarth, transport, environment and pinned mirror snapshots. Launch one web worker on an unused localhost port with API_RATE_LIMIT=10000 and the default 60-second window. Create a personal key and supply it through BHARATOS_BENCHMARK_KEY. Run python -m scripts.measure_performance with --url, --configuration and a new --output file. Repeat with --limit 12 and a second output file. Use a separate key or wait for the quota window if repeating multiple runs. A test quota override belongs in the isolated test process.

docs.title: 5 November prototype baseline
docs.text:
The recorded run in local-prototype.json measured one Windows localhost process on 5 November 2026. The server used one Uvicorn worker, in-memory scheme snapshots and the demonstration key; PostgreSQL, Redis and rate limiting were not enabled. Client and server shared the same machine. This is a baseline for the prototype, not a production capacity estimate.

Each concurrency level ran 500 GET requests to /api/v1/schemes, after one warm-up request. The p95 is the nearest-rank 95th percentile of client-observed request latency, including failed requests; time waiting for the benchmark's concurrency semaphore is excluded. Error rate counts anything other than HTTP 200, including connection errors. Provenance coverage is the fraction of successful responses containing source and verification fields in metadata and in each record.

Concurrent requests Successful / total p95 latency Error rate Provenance coverage 10 500 / 500 54.74 ms 0% 100% 50 500 / 500 858.19 ms 0% 100% 100 500 / 500 2,204.37 ms 0% 100% 500 500 / 500 3,294.57 ms 0% 100%

This is a single short run with 500 samples per level. The large p95 increase under higher concurrency is a finding to investigate, not proof of a universal performance limit. Repeat runs are required. A developer time-to-first-call pilot has not been conducted. The pilot protocol provides a repeatable task and outcome summary procedure; it contains no participant results.

docs.title: PostgreSQL and Redis run
docs.text:
The separate local-postgres-redis.json run on 8 November 2026 used a Windows HTTP client and one Docker-hosted Uvicorn worker, PostgreSQL 17.11, Redis 7.4.12, eight curated scheme snapshots, and an intentionally raised API quota of 5,000 requests per 60 seconds. The cache was warmed before the measured levels. This is a local single-run result, not a production capacity claim.

Concurrent requests Successful / total p95 latency Error rate Provenance coverage 10 500 / 500 48.98 ms 0% 100% 50 500 / 500 877.24 ms 0% 100% 100 500 / 500 1,799.95 ms 0% 100% 500 500 / 500 3,167.86 ms 0% 100%

Redis reported 4,001 cache hits and one miss after the warm-up and 2,000 measured requests; the list route read the catalogue twice per request in that run. PostgreSQL recorded 2,001 API calls, including warm-up. These are cache-operation counters, not one count per API request. The two runs used different application revisions and execution environments, so their numbers are not a controlled before-and-after comparison. Repeat tests, larger real datasets, different worker counts and a multi-client setup are needed for reliable capacity conclusions.

The isolated benchmark containers and their test-only database volume were removed after the run.

docs.title: Single catalogue-read follow-up
docs.text:
After removing the second catalogue read from each list request, a further run on 8 November 2026 used the same stated local PostgreSQL/Redis configuration and 500 requests per level. The raw results are in local-postgres-redis-single-read.json.

Concurrent requests Successful / total p95 latency Error rate Provenance coverage 10 500 / 500 56.13 ms 0% 100% 50 500 / 500 754.48 ms 0% 100% 100 500 / 500 1,975.55 ms 0% 100% 500 500 / 500 3,502.71 ms 0% 100%

Redis recorded 2,000 hits and one miss for the 2,001 calls including warm-up, confirming one catalogue-cache lookup per call. The previous run recorded 4,001 hits and one miss. Latencies improved at one level and worsened at others; one run of each is insufficient to infer a performance improvement. The isolated follow-up containers and their test-only database volume were removed after measurement.

The separate service integration verification records functional checks against real PostgreSQL and Redis; it is not a load benchmark.

The separate backup and recovery drill records a local PostgreSQL dump and restore into a new database.

The scheduler verification records a Compose run using a synthetic snapshot; it does not establish that an official file was imported.

The local HTTPS verification covers a development CA and a verified localhost connection, not public deployment.

The source-check verification records administrator-triggered HEAD results and their limitations.

The scheme-search verification records SQLite and PostgreSQL filter and migration checks; it is not a large-dataset benchmark.

The historical PIN mirror import records a full-file integration check, source limitations and the behavior when records already belong to another adapter.

The local launcher verification records first-start and restart behavior using an isolated SQLite database.

To repeat the baseline, start the server with no DATABASE_URL or REDIS_URL in one terminal:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8767

In another terminal:

$env:BHARATOS_BENCHMARK_KEY = "bharatos_demo_2026"
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m scripts.measure_performance --output tmp\performance.json --configuration "Single local worker; in-memory prototype"

The harness only permits localhost targets. Database-backed runs require a valid developer API key and must report the active rate limit, cache state, worker count and dataset size. The output does not include the API key. Do not compare the results with this baseline without recording the configuration and client/server environment.

docs.title: Recent service verification
docs.text: 15 November 2026: PostgreSQL, Redis and image checks.

docs.title: Developer time-to-first-call pilot
docs.text: Status: not yet conducted. This protocol and the summarizer do not represent participant results. Run the study with real volunteers and record actual observations before reporting it.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
1. Recruit a small convenience sample of developers or computing students. Participation is voluntary; explain the task, the anonymous data recorded and that they may stop at any time.
  2. Use a disposable local database initialized with scripts.start_local --db PATH --skip-mirror. Prepare a separate fresh database for each participant so existing accounts, keys and usage do not affect the task. Use synthetic email addresses and passwords; do not record credentials.
  3. Give each person the same starting page (/developers) and access to the same documentation. Record the project version, configuration, date, dataset size, sample size and timeout in the final report. Do not give step-by-step help unless requested; record any assistance.

docs.title: Task and measurement
docs.text:
Read the same instruction to everyone: “Using the supplied documentation, create a developer account and API key, then make a successful authenticated request for the scheme list. Show the HTTP status and identify the source field in the response.” Start a stopwatch when the participant first sees the developer page. Stop at the first HTTP 200 response whose data and meta.source are visible, using the participant's personal key. Both the playground and a direct HTTP client are acceptable. A demo key or unauthenticated response does not meet the task.

Use a fixed 10-minute limit. Record completion time in whole seconds, whether assistance occurred, and whether the task completed, timed out, or was voluntarily stopped. Do not count a 401, a partial response or an account creation as completion. Stop the clock at the limit for a timeout; record the actual elapsed time if the participant stops earlier. Do not enter names, emails, API keys, session tokens, screen recordings or other identifying information in the observations file.

docs.title: Record and summarize
docs.text:
Create a private JSON file outside the repository using the structure below. The values shown are format examples only; replace them with real observed values and never present them as results.

{
  "timeout_seconds": 600,
  "observations": [
    {"outcome": "completed", "elapsed_seconds": 145, "assistance": false},
    {"outcome": "timed_out", "elapsed_seconds": 600, "assistance": true}
  ]
}

Run .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m scripts.summarize_pilot PATH_TO_OBSERVATIONS.json. The command prints participant and outcome counts, completion rate, and median completion times for all successful participants and for the unassisted subset. Failed or stopped attempts are reported separately and are not included in the median; their elapsed times are censored, not completed times. If nobody completes, the corresponding median is null.

Report the number recruited and completing, all assistance and stop counts, both medians and the time limit. Describe recruitment and any disruptions. A small convenience sample is exploratory; it does not establish population-wide performance. Store private notes securely, retain them only as needed for the course, and publish only aggregated, non-identifying results with permission.

docs.title: Local backup and recovery drill — 8 November 2026
docs.text:
An isolated Compose project using PostgreSQL 17.11 was migrated and populated with eight curated scheme snapshots and three sample PIN records. A custom-format pg_dump archive was created using scripts.database_backup and restored into a newly created database.

The original and recovered databases each contained 11 normalized records and reported Alembic revision 20261105_06. A second restore attempt using the same target database was refused by createdb before pg_restore ran. The original database was not modified by the restore.

The first drill exposed a buffered-input stream positioning problem. The restore command was corrected to pass an unbuffered, rewound file descriptor to pg_restore, and the successful restore above was repeated into a different new database. Automated tests cover the stream position, invalid input, overwrite protection and the create-before-restore sequence.

The isolated Compose containers and test database volume were removed after the drill. This confirms a local recovery exercise for sample data; it does not replace an operational backup schedule, encrypted off-host storage or a documented production cutover and recovery-time test.

docs.title: Local launcher verification — 14 November 2026
docs.text:
The scripts.start_local launcher was run with a new SQLite database in the ignored tmp directory and the pinned 2024 third-party PIN mirror available in data/raw/. It created the database, applied migrations and imported eight curated schemes, 14 historical PIB scheme records, three curated PINs and 19,297 additional mirror PINs. The three existing curated PIN records were preserved. The resulting database contained 22 schemes and 19,300 PIN records.

A test developer registered and made an authenticated request for mirror PIN 515631. The API returned 15 offices with third_party_mirror provenance, last_verified: null and review_due freshness. The local server was stopped and restarted against the same database; the launcher reported that it reused the database without reimporting records.

Automated tests cover initial setup without the mirror, checksum failure without publishing a partial database, preservation of unrelated or outdated databases, and source ownership when a mirror overlaps existing PINs. The test database remains in the ignored tmp directory and contains only sample data and a test account. The historical mirror is not independently verified against the current official directory.

docs.title: Local HTTPS verification — 8 November 2026
docs.text:
An isolated Compose project started PostgreSQL, Redis, the migrated application and the optional Caddy TLS proxy on separate localhost ports. The proxy generated a certificate for localhost using its internal development CA; automatic installation into the host trust store was disabled.

A Python TLS client supplied with the exported public root certificate successfully verified the certificate chain and hostname and retrieved /health/ready, which reported PostgreSQL and Redis as ready. A client using the unmodified system trust store rejected the untrusted local CA, as expected. Windows curl with its Schannel backend reported that revocation status was unknown when the local root was supplied; the documented Python verification method succeeded without changing the system trust store.

The isolated containers, test PostgreSQL volume and Caddy private CA volumes were removed after the drill. A copy of the test CA's public root remains in the ignored local tmp directory. No host trust settings were changed. This test does not validate public DNS, public certificates, internet exposure, external proxy configuration or production security.

docs.title: Historical PIN mirror import — 14 November 2026
docs.text:
The official OGD page's download could not be obtained in this environment. A third-party GitHub mirror was downloaded separately; its repository claims the CSV originated from the Department of Posts dataset. The copy has not been compared against an official file, and its current accuracy is not established. Its repository commit date is 5 May 2024, which is not proof of the date of the underlying postal data.

The downloaded CSV's SHA-256 is 84af12fa29adddedfa9addcf46546000d89d2e2899b2993dc88050fafc8861e2. A structural scan found 157,126 rows and 19,300 distinct six-digit PINs. The raw CSV and local provenance note are in the ignored data/raw/ folder, not in Git.

docs.title: Import checks
docs.text:
• A migrated, isolated SQLite database imported 19,300 PIN records. Reimporting the same file succeeded without increasing the record count.
  • Sample PINs 147004, 110001 and 560001 had six, 23 and ten post-office entries in this mirror copy. An authenticated API request for 147004 returned its offices with provenance_kind: third_party_mirror, review_reason: unverified_mirror, last_verified: null and snapshot_date: 2024-05-05.
  • In a separate PostgreSQL test stack seeded with three curated PIN records, the mirror import applied 19,297 records and preserved the three records owned by the curated adapter. An authenticated API request for mirror PIN 515631 returned 15 offices and the same unverified provenance and null verification date.
  • The full test suite subsequently passed 91 tests with PostgreSQL and Redis services, including snapshot omission handling. The isolated PostgreSQL test volume was then removed.

The isolated SQLite database remains in the ignored tmp directory and contains only test accounts and data. This exercise demonstrates a working historical-mirror import; it is not an official full-directory verification or a claim that any listed PIN is currently valid.

docs.title: Local scheduler verification — 8 November 2026
docs.text:
An isolated Compose project ran the optional ingestion profile with PostgreSQL 17 and a read-only, synthetic one-row CSV fixture. The configured checksum matched the file; the scheduler reported a successful import, and PostgreSQL stored one PIN record with the supplied 2026-09-01 verification date and review_due freshness status.

This drill verifies the Compose service, file mount, database connection and first scheduled run. The fixture is synthetic: it is not an official PIN-directory import. Unit tests separately cover unchanged snapshots, checksum mismatch, missing files and recovery after failure. The isolated containers and test database volume were removed after the drill; the fixture remains in the ignored local tmp directory.

docs.title: Scheme search verification — 13 November 2026
docs.text:
The SQLite suite compares database-backed filtering with the original Python filtering for text, category, state and audience combinations, case folding, and literal % and _ characters. It also checks that reimport updates the index and that upgrading an existing database backfills the index without deleting canonical records.

An isolated Docker Compose project with PostgreSQL 17 and Redis 7 ran the full suite with live service tests: 84 passed. A separate new PostgreSQL database was migrated to the previous revision, populated with one scheme fixture, and upgraded to the current revision. Searching the backfilled index returned the expected record. The isolated test containers and database volume were removed afterwards.

These tests establish functional behavior for the exercised records, not a performance claim for large datasets. Category and state/audience values are indexed; free-text substring matching still uses SQL LIKE and may require a dedicated full-text index as the catalogue grows.

docs.title: Local service integration verification — 8 November 2026
docs.text: An isolated Docker Compose project was used to verify the current application build. It used PostgreSQL 17.11, Redis 7.4.12, Docker Engine 29.9.2, Python 3.13.18 and pytest 8.4.2. The PostgreSQL database contained only the eight curated scheme snapshots and three sample PIN records. No official bulk dataset or real personal information was imported.

docs.title: Observed results
docs.text:
• The application image built, both service health checks passed, and Alembic upgraded an empty PostgreSQL database to the latest revision.
  • Snapshot ingestion produced eight scheme records and three PIN-code records.
  • The full pytest suite ran in a separate disposable container against the PostgreSQL and Redis services: 56 passed, including the three service-integration tests.
  • The web container reported both configured dependencies as ready.
  • A test developer registered, signed in, created a key, retrieved the scheme list and PIN 147004, exceeded an intentionally reduced two-request quota and received 429.
  • The developer usage endpoint counted three authenticated calls, including the rejected call. Revoking the key caused the next request to return 401.
  • The administrator endpoint reported Redis cache metrics as available, with one hit and one miss in this small smoke test.

These checks verify the observed local configuration only. They do not establish production security, availability, throughput or source-data accuracy. The separate performance baseline in local-prototype.json was measured in in-memory mode, not against this service stack.

After the test, the isolated test containers, network and test database volume were removed. The pre-existing application on port 8000 was not changed.

docs.title: Local PostgreSQL and Redis verification — 15 November 2026
docs.text:
The current application was tested against isolated disposable containers running PostgreSQL 17.11 and Redis 7.4.12, with host ports bound to localhost. The database began empty; Alembic upgraded it through revision 20261115_09, and the curated seed imported eight schemes and three PIN samples. The full host-side pytest suite ran with both service URLs configured: 108 passed, including five opt-in service tests. Subsequently, the transport and environment snapshot import commands each successfully inserted one record into that PostgreSQL database.

The Docker image also built successfully. Running each of the transport and environment import commands with --help inside that image confirmed that both scripts were packaged and importable. This check does not demonstrate a populated PostgreSQL upgrade from an older revision; that backfill path was exercised with SQLite at that point. A subsequent isolated PostgreSQL test exercised the populated upgrade from 20261113_08: a duplicate slug stopped the migration, removing the duplicate allowed backfill, a conflicting insert failed against the unique index, and downgrade removed the index column. The original fixture record remained unchanged. The test used a uniquely named temporary schema, which it removed afterward. It also does not establish production security or government data accuracy. The database contained test and curated sample data only.

To repeat the populated PostgreSQL migration test, point TEST_POSTGRES_MIGRATION_URL at a disposable PostgreSQL database whose user can create and drop schemas, then run python -m pytest tests/test_postgres_migration.py. The test creates and deletes only its own randomly named schema; do not point it at a production database.

docs.title: Administrator source-check verification — 13 November 2026
docs.text:
An isolated SQLite database and local server were used to test the administrator-triggered HTTP HEAD checks. The API and browser dashboard both loaded the recorded results. In one observed run, the OGD PIN resource page and PFRDA page returned HTTP 200, myScheme returned 405 for HEAD, and the PIB release returned 401 for HEAD. These are observations from this environment at the recorded time, not statements about the current availability of the services.

Checks use a fixed list of official URLs, do not follow redirects or read response bodies, and record only the result, HTTP status, check time and duration. A page returning 200 does not verify the downloadable dataset or its contents. A rejected HEAD request does not prove that an ordinary browser request or dataset download will fail. Automated tests use mocked responses to cover authorization, redirects, access restrictions, network failures and persistence.

The isolated SQLite test database remains in the ignored tmp directory. It contains test monitoring records only and no user credentials.

The latest migration was also applied to an isolated PostgreSQL 17 database, where four mocked probe results were written and read successfully. The full suite ran in a disposable container with PostgreSQL and Redis: 66 tests passed, including the service-integration tests. The isolated container stack and its test database volume were removed after verification.
